speaker: HOST_A
text: So today we’re diving into the wild world of corpus design—basically, how you decide what texts to feed your language model so it doesn’t grow up confused.

speaker: HOST_B
text: Right, and the first thing the lecture hammered home is that you can’t just scoop up random tweets and call it a day; you’ve got to decide up front whether you’re building a social-media chatbot, a medical question-answerer, or the next great Hindi conversational agent.

speaker: HOST_A
text: Exactly, and that choice colors everything—if you only crawl Bollywood forums, your bot will sound like a filmi dialogue writer, which is awesome until someone asks it about diabetes symptoms.

speaker: HOST_B
text: And then there’s the whole “homo-lingual versus multilingual” angle: one language keeps life simple, but the second you add a second language you need sentence-level alignment or at least comparable documents, otherwise your translations come out like word salad.

speaker: HOST_A
text: Yeah, the lecture warned that comparable corpora don’t have to be perfect mirrors, but if the domains drift too far—say, Hindi Wikipedia versus English tweets—you’ll teach the model that “python” means both a snake and a programming language in the same breath.

speaker: HOST_B
text: Speaking of messy data, the privacy minefield came up next. Anytime you scrape dialogues from Reddit or WhatsApp leaks, you’re one regex away from leaking phone numbers, and once that’s in the wild you can’t stuff it back in the bottle.

speaker: HOST_A
text: So the rule of thumb is strip first, ask later: anonymize names, replace digits, nuke the emojis that can geolocate someone—basically treat every corpus like it’s going to end up on the front page of the newspaper.

speaker: HOST_B
text: And if you’re lucky enough to find pre-cleaned “anonymous data,” you still need to eyeball it, because the lecture hinted that even “public” forums can hide personal stories that feel icky once you actually read them.

speaker: HOST_A
text: Once the data’s ethically squeaky, you hit the next fork: supervised versus unsupervised. If you want the model to learn that “artificial intelligence” is a collocation, you can either feed it labeled examples or let it count co-occurrences and hope statistics do the heavy lifting.

speaker: HOST_B
text: That’s where those PMI and T-score formulas swagger in. PMI loves the rare but meaningful duos—like “strong tea”—while T-score gives frequent pairs like “New York” their due without letting them drown everything else.

speaker: HOST_A
text: And the lecture swears by LLR—log-likelihood ratio—as the new kid on the block, because it balances both ends of the spectrum without the voodoo hand-tuning that PMI sometimes needs.

speaker: HOST_B
text: But before any math happens, you still have to preprocess: tokenize, lowercase, lemmatize, or you’ll treat “Tea” and “tea” as two different words and miss the collocation entirely.

speaker: HOST_A
text: Right, and don’t forget the n-gram step; if you only look at bigrams, you’ll never catch “salt and pepper” as a trigram collocation, and your dinner-bot will sound like it’s never seen a kitchen.

speaker: HOST_B
text: Once you’ve got clean, domain-specific, ethically-sanitized, language-tagged data, the lecture says you still need to balance the dialects—formal news for politeness, social media for slang, maybe some scientific abstracts if you want it to sound smart at parties.

speaker: HOST_A
text: And if you’re building that Hindi chatbot example they walked through, you’d deliberately mix Bollywood subtitles for tone, government FAQs for facts, and customer-support logs for question-answer structure, then run collocation stats so it knows “kaise ho” is casual while “aap kaise hain” is respectful.

speaker: HOST_B
text: The beauty is that all of these decisions—domain, language count, privacy scrubbing, collocation measure—get baked into the corpus metadata, so six months later you don’t stare at your model and wonder why it thinks “coronavirus party” is a normal phrase.

speaker: HOST_A
text: So bottom line: corpus design isn’t data entry, it’s editorial choices all the way down, and every shortcut you take shows up later like a typo in a tattoo.

speaker: HOST_B
text: To wrap, the lecture left us with a cheat-sheet: pick your domain first, anonymize second, balance genres third, then let PMI, T-score, or LLR tell you which word pairs are glued together by meaning rather than coincidence; do that and your model will sound less like a random sentence generator and more like someone you’d actually want to chat with.
